title: Possessive Predicate
definition: A [term:predicate] that expresses that one referent possesses another. Languages employ several strategies: (1) the locative strategy, where the possessor is encoded as a locative and the possessed item is the grammatical subject ('a match is at me'); (2) the genitive/nominal strategy, where the possessed item is predicated as belonging to a genitive possessor ('it is my car'); (3) the existential strategy, where the possessed item 'exists' with the possessor as an oblique; and (4) the HAVE-verb strategy, where possession is treated as a transitive relation. HAVE drift describes a typological tendency for the possessor in existential-based constructions to shift from oblique toward nominative/topic over time.

examples.translation: Lapsel on piima. ('The child has milk.' Lit: 'Milk is at the child.')
examples.notes: Locative strategy: possessor takes locative case; the possessed item is the nominative subject of the copula on.

examples.translation: Dir mašina b-ugo. ('I have a car.' Lit: 'It is my car.')
examples.notes: Genitive/nominal strategy: the possessed item is predicated as belonging to a genitive possessor. The copula ugo agrees in noun class with mašina (class b).

examples.translation: Cocugun babasi var. ('The child has a father.' Lit: 'The child's father exists.')
examples.notes: Existential strategy: the possessed item (babasi 'his/her father') is the subject of the existential particle var; the possessor is a genitive NP modifying it.

The HAVE-verb strategy treats possession as a transitive relation, with the possessor as subject (A role) and the possessed as object. This is typologically unusual — most of the world's languages use one of the oblique-possessor strategies.

examples.translation: 나는 책이 있다. (na-nïn chæk.i iss-da) ('I have a book.' Lit: 'As for me, a book is.')
examples.notes: HAVE drift: the possessor na 'I' bears the topic marker -nïn rather than a locative/genitive, having drifted toward the subject/topic role over time. The possessed chæk.i 'book' retains the nominative subject.
